lesson.title: Putting Numbers on Chance: What a Random Variable Really Is
lesson.summary: A random variable assigns exactly one numerical value to every outcome of a random phenomenon, turning chance outcomes into numbers you can compute with and eventually attach probabilities to.
lesson.body:
A variable is any characteristic that can take different values across individuals or trials, and a random phenomenon is a process whose individual outcomes are uncertain but which settles into a regular long run pattern. A random variable, usually written as a capital letter such as X, is the bridge between those two ideas: it is a rule that assigns exactly one number to every possible outcome of a random phenomenon. Once outcomes are numbers instead of labels like heads or girl, you can add them, average them, graph them, and eventually attach a probability to each possible value, which is what a probability distribution does.

Random variables come in two broad types. A discrete random variable has a countable list of possible values, such as the number of heads in a fixed number of flips or the number of siblings a person has. A continuous random variable can take any value in an interval, such as an exact height or an exact waiting time. Everything in this course so far has been discrete, and that is where the next examples stay.

Here is a worked example. Flip a fair coin 3 times and let X stand for the number of heads. There are 8 equally likely outcomes in the sample space: HHH, HHT, HTH, THH, HTT, THT, TTH, TTT. Assign the value of X to each one by counting its heads: HHH gives X equals 3; HHT, HTH, and THH each give X equals 2; HTT, THT, and TTH each give X equals 1; TTT gives X equals 0.

Group the outcomes by their X value to get a distribution. X equals 0 happens for exactly 1 outcome out of 8, so P(X equals 0) is 1/8. X equals 1 happens for 3 outcomes, HTT, THT, TTH, so P(X equals 1) is 3/8. X equals 2 happens for 3 outcomes, HHT, HTH, THH, so P(X equals 2) is 3/8. X equals 3 happens for 1 outcome, HHH, so P(X equals 3) is 1/8. As a check, these probabilities should cover every outcome exactly once: 1/8 plus 3/8 plus 3/8 plus 1/8 equals 8/8, which is 1.

This little table is doing the same job that counting paths on a tree diagram or counting successful trials in a simulation did earlier, converting a random phenomenon into numbers you can summarize. A random variable simply gives that conversion a name and a formal structure, setting up everything that follows about probability distributions.
